plain: Should government take more steps to make sure everyone has health insurance, even if taxpayers pay more? In practice that means federal premium tax credits, Medicaid and state help.
agree_means: Supports keeping or expanding public help with coverage, such as restoring the enhanced ACA premium credits and protecting Medicaid, and accepts higher public spending.
disagree_means: Prefers less public spending on coverage, such as limits on federal subsidies and Medicaid or more reliance on private markets, and accepts that fewer people may be covered.

now.text: The enhanced federal premium tax credits, which lowered marketplace premiums, ended December 31, 2025. The U.S. House voted 230 to 196 in January 2026 to revive them for three years. In late September 2026, Colorado's insurance commissioner was still asking Congress to restore them.

research_notes: Claude in Chrome was not connected this session, so the one blocked page, the CBO report (cbo.gov/publication/61734, bot-protected), was read in the built-in Browser pane instead; its source carries via: browser. All other pages were fetched directly and every quote was checked against the fetched text. Double-check: (1) The 377,000 figure is the number of expansion adults subject to the new rules, not a projected loss; the state expects about 175,000 to need to act (Denver7, Sept 2026). No official Colorado estimate of how many will actually lose Medicaid was found. The 2025 HCPF slide (PDF) says 377K could face mid-year coverage loss. (2) Enrollment: the Colorado Sun gives about 1.2 million in Oct 2025; Denver7 says 1.1 million; text uses the Sun figure. (3) The Division of Insurance releases carry political framing (they blame Congressional Republicans); only factual sentences are quoted. The 75,000 coverage-loss figure is the Division's own projection; actual 2026 exchange enrollment fell only 2% (that is plan sign-ups, not total insured). (4) The $19.2 billion / $5.75 billion budget figures are the Joint Budget Committee's April 2026 proposal, not necessarily the final appropriation. (5) Paragon's improper-enrollment estimate is contested; a fetchable rebuttal (for example from KFF) was not found, so none is cited. (6) Whether Congress acted on the credits after the Sept 22, 2026 Division release was not checked; the web-search allowance ran out mid-run, so the last few topics were researched from direct page fetches only. (7) The Ballotpedia and KUNC pages are news summaries; the CBO cost figure is for a permanent extension enacted Sept 30, 2025.
